mitigation_mechanism: These are programme-scale or unspecified soil and water conservation packages. A review of impact studies finds such methods particularly useful in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability, Ethiopia's PSNP public works improved watershed drought resilience by increasing water availability, and in semi-arid Brazil production cisterns can reduce animal mortality in severe drought [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_drought_hazard_arega24_4, ev_drought_hazard_castro22_2]. Physical soil and water conservation structures were also reported to buffer crop growth against the 2015 severe drought in Ethiopia, and a water-harvesting review states that dry spells can be bridged through investments in water management [ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1, ev_crop_yield_rock10_1]. In Burkina Faso, zaï of 30–40 cm and 1-m half-moon plots mitigated the impact of dry spells by retaining moisture for 2-3 weeks [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. A Burkina Faso review concludes that soil and water conservation techniques helped reduce vulnerability to drought and famine [ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7].
caveats: The same review states that crop yields cannot be sustained during a meteorological drought and different coping mechanisms are required [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. The PSNP note adds that vegetation greenness still followed local drought severity, Niger families with soil and water conservation still had an estimated 28 percent deficit in low-rainfall years, and in Tunisia four consecutive drought years limited soil-conservation benefits [ev_drought_hazard_arega24_4, ev_food_security_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_iegtun13_1]. Every unit is a bundled programme, pooled soil and water conservation or an expert review, so the share due to water harvesting is not isolated; the Brazilian statement describes potential without data and the Ethiopian 2015 finding is a secondary citation [ev_drought_hazard_castro22_2, ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]. The Burkina Faso half-moon and zaï moisture finding is the authors' statement about dry spells, for pits filled with compost [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. mitigation_mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. Conservation agriculture meta-analyses find immediate positive yield effects when water stress occurs during crop growth, because mulch improves the soil water balance, and maize yields under conservation agriculture generally above conventional practice in seasons with a precipitation balance below 200 mm, rising as conditions get drier [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; in Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis also report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the contrast was 1520 against 400 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In Zambia, a review of conservation agriculture cites trial findings that higher soil moisture improved yields in poor seasons, showing the potential to reduce the risk of crop failure due to low or poorly distributed rainfall [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]. In on-farm conservation-farming trials in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia the largest yield difference over conventional ploughing came in rainy seasons with low rainfall, when the practice maximises rainfall infiltration so the crop can bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season of very scattered rainfall, maize in hand-hoe conservation-farming basins yielded 3,054 kg per hectare against 1,339 kg under ploughing, which the authors say showcased the water-harvesting benefits of the basins [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather put the first-year maize difference between conservation agriculture and ploughing largely in seasons with below normal rainfall, and in the 1980/81 drought year 241 mm produced some maize grain under conservation agriculture and none under ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated out-yielded tilled rice on hillside fields in three seasons that each had a month-long rainfall deficit [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. A commercial farmer in South Africa reported that his no-till, residue-cover and rotation system completely buffered his farm from mild droughts or dry spells through increased rainfall infiltration [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10].
caveats: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Kenyan trial's short rains with meteorological droughts, tied ridging gave no advantage (0.52 against 0.53 t per hectare without inputs, 1.17 against 1.27 with manure and fertiliser) because there was little or no rainwater to hold in the basins [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. In Mozambique maize and cowpea failed completely on all treatments in the drought season, in long-term Zimbabwe trials mulched and reduced-tillage maize yielded considerably less than conventional tillage in extreme seasons, conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect on maize in a Kenyan season with a failed start, and a study cited in a meta-analysis reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7, ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The family now rests partly on conservation agriculture meta-analyses and on-farm or trial measurements in Malawi, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Mozambique; the zaï and tassa contrasts are author estimates, the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the Kenyan tied-ridging result is a single-site trial [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. Water harvesting is not irrigation, and the new primaries mark the limit: at the more arid Kenyan sites of Laikipia and Machakos each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, with 0 kg per hectare of maize harvested at Machakos due to meteorological drought, and the conservation-farming treatments did not avert it [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The crop model shows the same limit: in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both conservation agriculture and ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the mulch-based system [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5], and in the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The East African low-rainfall gain is for the best system per site, ripping or pitting usually with fertiliser, so it is bundled with reduced tillage and fertiliser, and the authors read it as a trend from their own figure [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. The Zambia 2001/2 basin contrast is a raw comparison in a single season with no normal-year reference, and most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit, so part of the gap is the input package [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The semi-arid drought-year gains are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting, not measured seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. The Madagascar dry-spell gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation and have no normal-year comparison [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. The South African statement is a single commercial farmer's before-and-after testimony for a residue-cover system with no capture structure [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10]. The Zambia review statement is cited secondhand, gives no magnitude and has no normal-year comparison, and the trial behind it bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3].

mitigation_mechanism: In semi-arid Burkina Faso and Niger, zaï pits and stone bunds let more water infiltrate and conserve soil moisture, so rainfed crops suffer less from dry spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_soil_water_retention_zoug14_1]. Zaï gave 300 – 400 kg of sorghum in a year of low rainfall where untreated land yielded 0 kg/ha, only fields treated with tassa produced a harvest in the 1990 drought year, and crops behind stone bunds could yield two to three times more than control plots during dry years [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_1_s]. In semi-arid Brazil, water from runoff ponds applied as supplemental irrigation during in-season dry spells has reduced farming risk in years of irregular rainfall, and production-cistern water can reduce animal mortality in periods of more severe drought [ev_drought_hazard_brito07_10, ev_drought_hazard_castro22_2]. In Burkina Faso, zaï of 30–40 cm and 1-m half-moon plots mitigated the impact of dry spells by retaining moisture for 2-3 weeks [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. A Burkina Faso review concludes that soil and water conservation techniques helped reduce vulnerability to drought and famine [ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7].
caveats: The buffer runs out in severe or prolonged drought: Brazilian subsurface dams tended to dry up through a rainless year and, because of their small size, do not withstand long droughts, which records no benefit rather than damage to the works, and Niger farm families with soil and water conservation still had an estimated deficit of 28 percent in years with low rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_2, ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_3, ev_food_security_kabo04_1]. The large yield contrasts are author estimates or a secondary citation rather than controlled measurements, the Niger deficit figure is itself cited from another study and does not isolate a single practice, and the Brazilian pond and cistern statements are an institutional assertion and a statement of potential without data from an upper-middle-income country [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_1_s, ev_food_security_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_brito07_10, ev_drought_hazard_castro22_2]. The Burkina Faso half-moon and zaï moisture finding is the authors' statement about dry spells, for pits filled with compost [ev_soil_water_retention_zour25h1_7]. That Burkina Faso conclusion is the author's overall judgement, with no measured drought-year contrast behind it [ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7].

mitigation_mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. Conservation agriculture meta-analyses find immediate positive yield effects when water stress occurs during crop growth, because mulch improves the soil water balance, and maize yields under conservation agriculture generally above conventional practice in seasons with a precipitation balance below 200 mm, rising as conditions get drier [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; in Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis also report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. In Zambia, a review of conservation agriculture cites trial findings that higher soil moisture improved yields in poor seasons, showing the potential to reduce the risk of crop failure due to low or poorly distributed rainfall [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather put the first-year maize difference between conservation agriculture and ploughing largely in seasons with below normal rainfall, and in the 1980/81 drought year 241 mm produced some maize grain under conservation agriculture and none under ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated out-yielded tilled rice on hillside fields in three seasons that each had a month-long rainfall deficit [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. A commercial farmer in South Africa reported that his no-till, residue-cover and rotation system completely buffered his farm from mild droughts or dry spells through increased rainfall infiltration [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10].
caveats: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm, so it does not address seasonal drought [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In Mozambique maize and cowpea failed completely on conservation agriculture and control plots alike in the drought season, with gains only from year two, and a study cited in a meta-analysis reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower than conventional tillage in wet years [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The conservation agriculture meta-analyses and the Malawi on-farm survey of ground cover give measured support, while the zaï and tassa yield contrasts are author estimates and the dry-year gains in the older meta-analysis are secondary citations [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The crop model shows the same limit: in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both conservation agriculture and ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the mulch-based system [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5], and in the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The semi-arid drought-year gains are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting, not measured seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. The Madagascar dry-spell gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation and have no normal-year comparison [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. The South African statement is a single commercial farmer's before-and-after testimony for a residue-cover system with no capture structure [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10]. The Zambia review statement is cited secondhand, gives no magnitude and has no normal-year comparison, and the trial behind it bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3].

mitigation_mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. mitigation_mechanism: Floods washed away scores of small dams in northern Ghana, 37.9% of boulder-faced log check dams in Ethiopia still failed after a high-magnitude runoff event, and when peak flows break check dams the stored sediment is released rapidly [ev_flood_damage_veno12_1, ev_check_dam_failure_fran21_2, ev_check_dam_failure_fran21_1]. A check-dam review cites structural failure from the impact of large boulders in extreme floods, and grassed earth gully check dams in Morocco are described as fragile during major floods and needing frequent winter maintenance [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1_av, ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1_av]. WOCAT compilers rate gully-plugging check dams in Nepal and check-dam ponds in Ethiopia as not coping well with floods and a haffir and gabion check dams in Somalia as coping moderately [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1493_2011_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1547_2012_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_7777_2026_flash_flood].
caveats: Other compilers rate check dams in Tunisia, China and India and sand dams in Kenya as coping well, and a masonry check dam in Ethiopia as coping very well with flash floods, so sensitivity varies with construction, and the Moroccan earth check dams depend on frequent maintenance [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1400_2011_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1537_2012_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_6716_2023_flash_flood, ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1_av]. mitigation_mechanism: Banquettes lack the capacity to absorb runoff from erosive rains and overflow, diversion channels fill with eroded soil and overflow in the heaviest storms, and torrential rain collapses terrace walls or carries small terraces away in mass movements [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_2, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_2, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_3, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_5]. caveats: Failure is tied to maintenance and setting: rarely maintained diversion systems generally fail after 4 to 10 years, terrace collapse is linked to abandonment, and the Rwandan mass movement happened on terraces without trees [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_2, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_3, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_5]. The literature hazards are erosive rains, torrential rain and mass movements mapped to flood and come as expert and modelled statements without failure rates, and the WOCAT units are practitioner judgements from technology sheets rather than records of damage [ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_2].
